To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pacemaker current (Ih) in the mouse sinoatrial node and the thalamocorticothalamic network is generated by the HCN2 channel, and that the absence of Ih in the thalamus causes spontaneous absence seizures in the mouse.
mice lacking the pacemaking HCN2 channel display absence epilepsy and cardiac sinus dysrhrhythmia.
HCN2 knockout mice exhibit spontaneous absence epilepsy and sinus dysrythmia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new aspect in epilepsy research, the role of ion channels in epilepsy.
the function of HCN channels and their role in cardiac and neuronal physiology.
the molecular mechanisms of cardiac and neuronal pacemaking.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the absence epilepsy in the mice is due to a loss of the pacemaker current in the thalamocortial neurons and that the sinus dysrhythmias is due to the loss of the pacemaking current in the sinoatrial node.
HCN2 is required for normal cardiac pacemaker activity, and that the absence of HCN2 results in a sinus dysrhythmias, which is the most common type of dysrhythmia.
the HCN2 channel is a major determinant of the resting membrane potentials in neurons and in the sinoatrial node.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the absence of HCN2 in mice results in a shift in the maximum diastole potential to more hyperpolarized potentials and this shift in the maximum diastric potential causes the cardiac dysrhythmia.

the absence of HCN2 in the brain leads to a shift in the membrane potential of thalamocortcal neurons to more hyperpolarized potentials, which leads to a loss of inhibition of the T type calcium current and thus to the absence seizures.
HCN2 is a pacemaker subunit for the heart and brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCN2 is the major determinant of the membrane resting potential and that it is required for regular rhythmicity in the heart and in the brain.
HCN channels are not just pacemakers but also important for the regulation of neuronal excitability.
HCN2 channels play an important role in the control of membrane resting potential and that they are required for regular cardiac sinus and thalamic rhythmicity.
